newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam lays down law for foreign journalists.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam lays down law for foreign journalists.

text.p: Vietnam announced regulations on Tuesday aimed at setting out formal controls over the activities of visiting and resident foreign journalists.
The move came less than a week after Hanoi refused to renew a visa for an American correspondent, effectively expelling him.

The Nhan Dan daily, the official Communist Party mouthpiece, said the new rules, which come into effect on December 1, set limits on the number of foreign correspondents allowed in Vietnam. It did not say what the limit was.
It said journalists would be required to carry a letter of permission for news activities or an officially-issued press card at all times while working.
Foreign organisations or companies seeking to issue a news release, hold a news conference, exhibition or photo display would have to get Culture Ministry approval in advance.
Details of the new regulations were not immediately available.
Vietnam opened its door to foreign correspondents in the late 1980s, allowing a number of overseas news organisations to establish bureaux in the capital, Hanoi.
But despite an obscure and previously unpublished system of regulations, media activities have remained tightly controlled.
Foreign journalists are seldom invited to news conferences, interviews with senior officials are rare, permission must be obtained for travel, and staff must be hired from the government.
Hanoi did not renew a visa last week for resident U.S. journalist Adam Schwarz of the Far Eastern Economic Review magazine. No reason was given.
